To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) orthoses are currently used in the clinic to provide passive or active assistance to patients with a variety of impairments; (2) current actuator technologies are not ideal for use in orthoses; and (3) emerging actuator technologies may be better suited to the needs of orthosis users.

The requirements for orthosis actuator technologies are that they be safe and reliable, have a high power-to-weight ratio, be low cost, be lightweight, be compact and modular, have a long lifespan, have a low energy consumption, and have low noise, vibration, and heat generation.

current orthosis actuator systems are not compliant, and therefore, they do not interact with users in a natural way; the actuator technologies that are currently used in orthotic applications are not designed specifically for human interaction; and new actuator technologies are emerging that have the potential to be used in compliant orthoses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of a wearable robotic orthosis that can provide assistance to a person during walking and that is comfortable, lightweight, and easy to don and doff.
the design of a wearable and compliant robotic orthosis that is capable of assisting and training users to improve their walking ability.
the design, development and testing of wearable, lightweight and safe actuator systems to enable the development of a new generation of wearable robotic orthoses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, although there are many actuator technologies that can be used to actuate orthosis, the most promising are smart materials, which are lightweight, low cost and have the potential to be wearable.
the current orthosis actuator technology is still far from ideal, and there is a clear need for further research and development in this area.
there are no current actuators that are capable of meeting the needs of a user centered design for robotic orthoses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, while there has been a significant amount of research on robotic orthoses in recent years, there are many challenges still to overcome before they are widely adopted.
, in the future, we will see the use of smart actuators in orthoses.

, to be successful in the long term, orthosis actuation technology must: be compliant, so that the actuator does not cause discomfort to the user; be wearable, to ensure that the user can move naturally; and be robust and safe, to avoid injury and ensure the actuator can be used for a long time.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the design of robotic orthoses should be informed by the needs and preferences of the users.
the actuator should be designed for a specific orthosis application, and that the actuator and the orthosis must be designed together.
the design of orthoses and their actuation systems must be user centered, with a particular focus on the user's physical and psychological needs.
